title: The Republic
author: Plato
openingText: Yesterday I went down to the Piraeus with Glaucon, the son of Ariston, to offer my prayers to the goddess (Bendis, the Thracian Artemis); and I also wanted to see how they would celebrate the festival, since it was a new one. I was delighted with the procession put on by the locals, but the Thracians' procession was just as beautiful, if not more so. After we had finished our prayers and taken in the spectacle, we turned back toward the city. Just then, Polemarchus, the son of Cephalus, happened to spot us from a distance as we were setting off home, and he told his servant to run ahead and ask us to wait for him. The servant caught hold of my cloak from behind and said, “Polemarchus wants you to wait.”
about: A festival in the Piraeus takes Socrates to a conversation about debts. Must you always return what a friend has entrusted to you, even if it is a weapon and your friend has lost his reason? The question grows. Why choose to be just if injustice pays? Across ten books, Socrates and his companions look for justice on two scales, first in a city they build in speech and then in an individual soul. Glaucon and Adeimantus keep pressing for answers even when they are inclined to agree with him.

angleCards.title: Who is speaking?
angleCards.text: Glaucon tells the story of a ring that makes its wearer invisible. He gives the strongest argument he knows against justice because he wants Socrates to answer it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to distinguish what a speaker believes from a position he is testing.

angleCards.title: The city in large letters
angleCards.text: Socrates suggests looking for justice in the city before looking for it in the individual. When do people lend the city their traits, and when does the argument run the other way?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to test the comparison between the city and the soul.

angleCards.title: What does the prisoner see?
angleCards.text: Follow the light from the fire to the sun, then follow the freed prisoner back down. What makes it hard to see at each transition?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the prisoner out of the cave and back again.

angleCards.title: Who gets to be a poet?
angleCards.text: The guardians hear stories about the gods in childhood. Later Socrates asks what Homer knew of the people and deeds in his poems.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare the discussions of poetry in Books III and X.

cast.name: Socrates
cast.description: He tells yesterday’s conversation in the first person. When he offers a definition, he often leaves it to someone else to put it to the test.

cast.name: Cephalus
cast.role: The elderly head of the house
cast.description: He values money as a means of paying debts to gods and people. When he returns to the sacrifices, his son inherits the conversation.

cast.name: Polemarchus
cast.description: He stops Socrates on the way home. Citing the poet Simonides, he defends giving each person what is due.

cast.name: Thrasymachus
cast.description: He interrupts to argue that justice is the advantage of the stronger. He challenges Socrates to supply an answer of his own.

cast.name: Glaucon
cast.description: He reopens the conversation just when Socrates thought it was over. He tells the story of the Lydian shepherd’s ring.

cast.name: Adeimantus
cast.description: He wants to hear what justice itself does to a soul. Later he asks what the guardians get out of being guardians.

acclaim.quote: The safest general characterization of the European philosophical tradition is that it consists of a series of footnotes to Plato.

whyItMatters.title: The weapon in safekeeping
whyItMatters.body: A single exception unsettles a reasonable rule about returning what is owed. Keep that weapon in mind as the speakers change what they mean by a debt.

whyItMatters.title: Three forces in one person
whyItMatters.body: Leontius wants to look at some corpses and also wants to turn away. When he finally looks, he grows angry with his eyes. Who is angry with whom?

whyItMatters.title: Who chooses a life?
whyItMatters.body: In the closing myth the souls encounter an array of possible lives. A lottery determines who goes first, but each soul must choose. The opening question of how to live returns as a story.
